opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the questions I find myself coming back to a lot, because I genuinely don't know the answer, and I think it's a really important one.

There's a version of the world where we already have enough data. We've run the Large Hadron Collider, we have decades of cosmological observations, and a smart enough system could look at all of it and say, "Here's the theory that explains everything, and here's why you missed it." Historically, a lot of big breakthroughs came less from new measurements and more from someone looking at existing results in a new way. Einstein didn't need a new particle accelerator; he needed a new way of thinking about things people had already seen.

Then there's the other version, which honestly might be more likely: the data we have just doesn't constrain the answer enough. Maybe there are many theories consistent with everything we've observed, and the only way to tell them apart is to build new instruments and run new experiments. In that world, even a superintelligence is bottlenecked by the physical world. It might be incredibly good at telling us *which* experiment to run, which would still be a huge acceleration, but it can't skip that step.

My intuition, and it's only an intuition, is that it'll be somewhere in between. AI will squeeze way more out of existing data than we have, because humans are limited in how much we can hold in our heads at once. But at some point it'll say, "I need you to go measure this." And I think that's actually a pretty exciting future: AI as a scientific collaborator that tells us where to look, not an oracle that makes experiment unnecessary.

The broader thing I'd say is that the moment an AI system produces genuinely new scientific knowledge, something humans didn't know and couldn't easily have figured out, will feel like a real turning point. Whether that first happens in physics, biology, or math, I'm not sure. But I think we're closer to it than most people expect.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a sufficiently capable system could derive major scientific knowledge from existing observations, then contrasts that with knowledge requiring new experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, and it's one of the questions I find most exciting. My honest answer is I don't know, but I think it's plausible, and that alone is pretty remarkable.

Here's the way I'd frame it. We have an enormous amount of data sitting around from the LHC, from cosmological surveys, from decades of experiments, and a big chunk of it has probably never been looked at with the kind of attention it deserves. There are almost certainly patterns in there that no human has found, just because there aren't enough physicists and there isn't enough time. So one version of this is pretty boring and I'd bet heavily on it: a very capable AI goes through the existing data, finds anomalies people missed, suggests new analyses, and that accelerates the field a lot.

The more interesting version is whether you can get something like a genuinely new theory, something at the level of what Einstein did, without new experiments. And there's a real argument for it. Einstein didn't run experiments. He thought very hard about data and ideas that already existed, and the constraints from the existing evidence were strong enough that a sufficiently clever mind could find the right answer. If you believe that intelligence was the bottleneck there, and I think it was, then more intelligence should help.

But I want to be careful. At some point physics is empirical. You can have the most beautiful theory in the world, and if the data you'd need to distinguish it from the alternatives doesn't exist yet, you're stuck. You need the collider or the telescope. I'd guess the AI will tell us pretty quickly which experiments are actually worth running and which ones aren't, which is itself huge, because those experiments cost billions of dollars.

So my bet is something like this: existing data gets us much further than people expect, and then there's a frontier where we need new instruments, and the AI helps us build them faster and smarter. I'd be surprised if we don't see at least one real physics result over the next few years that comes primarily from a model looking at data everyone already had. And I think when that happens, it'll change how people think about what these systems are.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether greater intelligence could derive a genuinely new theory from existing data without new experiments, and says existing data could get us much further than expected.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible, but I don’t know. There may be insights hiding in the data we already have that humans just haven’t been smart enough to extract. A sufficiently capable AI could find those, and that would be an extraordinary result.

But intelligence doesn’t necessarily substitute for missing information. If two theories make the same predictions for every experiment we’ve done, you may still need a new experiment to distinguish them. So the question is: are we bottlenecked on intelligence, or are we bottlenecked on data? I’d be very excited to find out that, for more of physics than we expect, it’s intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether physics is bottlenecked on intelligence or data and says AI might uncover insights in existing data, directly raising how much knowledge intelligence can extract without new experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I don’t know. There may be discoveries sitting in the data we already have that we’re just not smart enough to see yet. An AI could find some connection or come up with a theory that makes everything click.

The harder question is whether the existing data contains enough information to distinguish that theory from other explanations. Intelligence can help you get much more out of the evidence, but it can’t necessarily replace a measurement you haven’t made. So I’d be very excited if AI could do this, but I wouldn’t assume that being sufficiently smart means you never need another experiment.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether existing data may contain undiscovered connections or theories, and contrasts what greater AI intelligence can extract from that evidence with the need for new measurements or experiments.
